pairs.rationale: Both passages describe Paul's being set apart and called in relation to proclaiming God's Son among the nations. Galatians adds the mother's-womb and revelation language; Romans adds slave and apostle designations. Their distinct descriptions are not merged into one quoted call scene.

Paul describes a gospel promised through prophets in holy Scriptures; Jesus explains scriptural necessity concerning the Christ and ensuing proclamation of repentance and forgiveness. Luke names Law, Prophets and Psalms. This compares the scriptural promise framework rather than claiming Romans supplies Luke's complete passage list.

Both gospel summaries identify Jesus with David's seed. Second Timothy also names His resurrection; Romans here qualifies Davidic descent according to the flesh. The additional clauses remain in their respective summaries rather than converting descent into the whole explanation of Sonship.

Acts links the fulfilled promise and God's raising Jesus with the psalm's Son declaration; Romans connects designation as Son of God in power with resurrection and the Spirit of holiness. The shared resurrection-and-Son relationship does not make the formulations identical or supply Acts with Romans' Spirit phrase.

Paul's later mission account describes Christ working through him to bring the nations to obedience in word and deed, with power and Spirit. This develops the opening apostleship-for-obedience mission, without making the later geographical itinerary an exhaustive list of all nations or replacing obedience of faith with a new formula.

The Roman addressees are called by Jesus Christ; the Corinthians are described as called into fellowship with God's Son. This compares the particular calling-and-belonging relation, while the communities and stated descriptions of their calling remain distinct.

Both addresses name a community's saintly calling and give grace and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. Rome and Corinth remain distinct audiences; the shared greeting does not identify their local circumstances or make the Corinthian sanctification clause an added Roman phrase.

Both notices describe a community's faith becoming widely known. Romans says in the whole world; the Thessalonian notice names Macedonia and Achaia and the report in every place. These are the texts' respective descriptions of renown, not a calculated identical audience or geographical statistic.

Paul's repeated remembrance and prayer for a community appear in both openings. Romans adds God as witness and service in the Son's gospel; Philippians specifies gratitude and joyful supplication. The same prayer pattern does not independently establish every prayer for the other community.

The closing appeal asks for prayer so Paul may reach the addressees by God's will, recalling the opening prayer for a permitted journey. The later Judean concerns and hoped-for refreshment supply its own circumstances rather than an invented schedule for the earlier petition.

The later expected visit with Christ's blessing and mutual refreshment develops Paul's desire to benefit the Roman community. It does not identify the opening spiritual gift as a specified charismatic ability or narrate the visit as already completed.

The Thessalonian report shows Paul himself encouraged through another community's faith; Romans hopes for encouragement through both sides' faith. The actual report and hoped-for mutual meeting differ, without reducing the Roman community to passive recipients.

Paul later again states that he has often been hindered from coming to the addressees. This explicitly recalls the unfulfilled travel plans. The later for-this-reason context is not used to reconstruct every earlier hindrance or an unreported attempted journey.

The mission obligation extends across different groups in both passages. Romans names Greek and non-Greek, wise and senseless; Corinthians describes Paul's service and adaptation among Jews, law-related groups and the weak. The lists and metaphors differ, and debtor does not specify a financial sum.

Paul's eagerness to proclaim in Rome corresponds to the Lord's instruction in Acts that he must also bear witness there. A declared intention and a narrated assurance are different utterances; Acts does not quote the letter's eagerness or supply every planned activity in Rome.

Both describe the proclaimed message as God's power in relation to salvation. Corinthians specifies the word of the cross and contrasts those perishing with those being saved; Romans specifies everyone believing, Jew first and Greek also. The descriptions are related without replacing either audience formulation.

Romans cites the righteous one's life by faith; the retained Habakkuk declaration says by My faithfulness after its drawing-back contrast. The first-person possessive and faith/faithfulness wording remain distinct. The correspondence does not replace the supplied Greek-based passage with a different Hebrew-derived formulation.

Both connect God's wrath with wrongdoing and disobedience. Romans speaks of revelation from heaven against ungodliness and suppression of truth; Ephesians warns against empty deception and wrath upon disobedience. Neither passage supplies an identical audience list or a newly calculated timetable for the other.

Wisdom argues from visible good things and created beauty toward their Maker, while Romans says God made what is knowable plain. This compares the explicit Creator-knowledge argument without treating every feature of Wisdom's account of error as Romans' own stated wording.

Both connect knowledge of the Maker through created things with accountability. Romans names invisible power and divinity; Wisdom reasons from greatness and beauty, first qualifies the blame as small, then says they are not excusable. Those qualifications remain alongside Romans' without-excuse statement rather than being erased.

Jeremiah describes fathers going after vanity and becoming vain; Romans describes failure to honor or thank God followed by futile reasoning. The turning-and-futility relation corresponds, while Jeremiah's ancestral accusation and Romans' wider account are not identified as the same historical group.

Both expose a reversal from claimed wisdom to foolishness. Corinthians directs the self-assessed wise to become foolish to be wise and cites God's assessment of worldly wisdom. Romans' idolatry setting and the Corinthian instruction remain distinct applications.

The psalm's exchange of glory for an animal likeness supplies a close textual image for Romans' glory-for-image exchange. The psalm specifies the calf; Romans lists human and multiple animal likenesses. The particular lists and historical scope are preserved rather than made identical.

Both describe being handed over in relation to impurity, but Romans names God as the one handing people over while Ephesians says they handed themselves over. The stated agents remain distinct; Ephesians' darkened-understanding description does not supply an additional bodily-dishonor clause.

The Lystra appeal directs people from vain objects to the living Creator of heaven, earth and sea; Romans contrasts worship of creation with the Creator. The particular attempted sacrifice and Romans' broader exchange account remain distinct, without identifying every form of creation worship with that crowd.

Likewise explicitly joins the following males' account to the females' exchange described here. The two descriptions and their stated actions remain distinct; the following verse's specified desire, acts and received penalty are not inserted as additional words about the females.

Leviticus supplies a prohibition concerning male-with-male intercourse; Romans describes males leaving relations with the female and male-with-male acts. This is a bounded comparison of the stated acts, with law-command and narrated indictment kept distinct; Leviticus is not presented as an explicit female-specific prohibition.

Both associate impaired mind or conscience with unfitting conduct and a damaged relation to knowledge or profession of God. Romans states God's handing over; Titus describes profession contradicted by works. Those agents and descriptions are not made identical.

Both catalogues name strife and envy or envies. Their order, contents and concluding warnings differ; Romans also names murder, while the retained Galatians list does not insert that term. The comparison neither fills omitted items from another edition nor identifies every hearer's conduct.

The catalogues share boasting, pride and disobedience to parents. Romans describes the current indictment; Second Timothy places its list in a warning about difficult times. The separate temporal settings and additional offences are preserved.

Both vice descriptions include absence of natural affection. The surrounding catalogue differs, and Romans' additional lack of understanding, faithfulness and mercy is not inserted into Second Timothy's particular sequence. This links a stated moral category rather than identifying the people as one group.

Jesus' servants comparison associates knowing the master's will and failing to act with heightened accountability; Romans describes knowledge of God's decree alongside wrongdoing and approval. The target does not independently state Romans' approval-of-others clause, and its contrasting servant penalties are not substituted for Romans' death wording.

Both warn that judgment of another implicates the person who judges. Matthew uses measure and beam/speck imagery; Romans explicitly charges the judge with practicing the same things. The images and forms of self-condemnation are preserved rather than making every act of judgment identical.

The psalm describes the Lord's judgment of the world with righteousness and peoples with truth; Romans calls God's judgment according to truth. This connects the stated standard of divine judgment without assigning the psalm's whole setting to Paul's particular interlocutor.

Both use a direct question about escaping judgment. Jesus names the judgment of Gehenna in His rebuke; Paul addresses a person who judges others while doing the same things. The audiences and specified judgment language are not silently equated.

Both link divine patience with repentance. Romans warns against despising kindness and forbearance; Second Peter explains the Lord's patience in relation to the promise and repentance. Neither turns patience into an assertion that every person has already repented.

Both use stored-up/future-repayment imagery for judgment. Romans says the hardened person stores wrath for himself; Deuteronomy speaks from God's side of stored things and repayment. The agents, objects and poem's particular enemies are not made identical.

The psalm states repayment to each according to works, corresponding to Romans' repayment declaration. Its surrounding language of God's mercy remains part of the retained passage; the cross-reference does not replace Paul's following account of the different outcomes.

Both connect continuing in good conduct with eternal life or the promised harvest. Galatians specifies sowing to the Spirit and not growing weary; Romans names seeking glory, honor and incorruptibility. The metaphors and stated conditions remain distinct, without adding an unstated complete account of salvation.

Both associate adverse divine judgment with disobedience. Romans contrasts disobedience to truth with obedience to unrighteousness; Second Thessalonians names disobedience to the gospel and not knowing God. Their descriptions and audiences remain distinct.

The later law distinction states that sin without law and sin under law both incur judgment, developing the all-person scope of the adverse outcome here. Law status and Jew/Greek designations remain distinct formulations rather than automatic identities for every individual.

Both describe God's favorable regard without limiting it to one national group. Romans names glory, honor and peace for good-doers; Peter speaks of acceptance in every nation for those fearing God and practicing righteousness. The respective outcomes and descriptions are not made identical.

Deuteronomy describes God as not showing partiality or taking gifts; Romans states that there is no partiality with God. The common divine standard does not transfer every surrounding Mosaic command into the wording of Paul's sentence.

The later summary charges both Jews and Greeks with being under sin, drawing together the preceding argument's groups. Romans2 here distinguishes sin without law and under law. The summary and distinction are related without making every legal-status term an exact ethnic synonym.

Both distinguish merely hearing from doing. Romans says the law's doers will be justified; James warns against self-deception and describes the continuing doer as blessed. Justified and blessed remain the texts' distinct claims, without replacing either with the other's wording.

The later conditional case of an uncircumcised person keeping the law's requirements develops the distinction between external possession and actual conduct. Gentile and uncircumcised remain different designations, and neither conditional example is made a claim that every Gentile perfectly keeps law.

Jeremiah promises God's laws put into understanding and written on hearts; Romans describes the law's work written in hearts, with conscience and reasoning. The shared heart-writing image does not identify every Gentile with the covenant's named house or turn work of the law into an identical quotation of My laws.

Both anticipate divine disclosure or judgment of hidden matters. Corinthians speaks of the Lord bringing hidden things to light and revealing heart counsels; Romans names God judging secrets through Christ Jesus. The praise language and particular apostolic setting remain distinct.

Paul elsewhere lists concrete Israelite and law-related credentials; Romans addresses a person claiming Jewish identity, resting on law and boasting in God. The comparison concerns stated privileges, without identifying the interlocutor as Paul or declaring that credentials guarantee right conduct.

Deuteronomy links keeping God's ordinances with wisdom and understanding; Romans describes knowledge and discernment through law instruction. The nations' appraisal in Deuteronomy and the interlocutor's claimed discernment are distinct settings, and knowledge is not substituted for the doing required in either context.

Both employ blind-guide imagery, with different force: Romans presents the person's confidence as a guide of the blind; Jesus calls the guides themselves blind and warns of the result. This compares the teaching image without identifying every member of the two audiences.

Both use instruction and infant-level learning imagery. Romans lists claimed teaching roles and law-based knowledge; Hebrews rebukes people who still need basic teaching and contrasts milk with mature discernment. The people and assessments are different rather than one identical teaching situation.

The no-stealing instruction recalled in Paul's question has its concrete legal counterpart in the command not to steal. Exodus supplies the prohibition, not an independent accusation that every teacher in Paul's audience has committed theft.

The adultery prohibition corresponds to the command explicitly invoked in Paul's question. The additional idol/temple-robbery question belongs to Romans and is not supplied as another clause of this retained Exodus command.

The following scriptural charge about God's name being blasphemed because of the addressees supplies the argument's stated consequence of dishonoring God through transgression. This is Paul's internal explanation, not an independent report proving every alleged offence of every person bearing the name Jew.

Paul marks this as written Scripture; Isaiah supplies the divine-name blasphemy among the nations language. The retained source's exact speaker, cause and surrounding clauses remain intact rather than being silently expanded to match Paul's shorter citation.

Both connect circumcision with obligation concerning the law. Romans conditions its benefit on practice and contrasts transgression; Galatians states the obligation to perform the whole law. The arguments' distinct clauses and settings are not collapsed into one sentence.

Both give weight to keeping God's requirements rather than treating the physical marker as sufficient. Corinthians says circumcision and uncircumcision are nothing but keeping commandments matters; Romans poses the uncircumcised keeper's being reckoned as circumcision. The formulations remain distinct.

Both present a judgment reversal against people with claimed advantages. Jesus names Ninevites' repentance and the southern queen's response to wisdom; Romans names an uncircumcised law-keeper. The judges, grounds and audiences remain distinct rather than making these groups identical.

The command concerning the heart supplies an interior counterpart to Romans' denial that the outward fleshly marker alone defines the matter. The Mosaic command and Paul's Jew/circumcision distinction are not identical formulations, and the target does not supply all of Romans' Spirit/letter argument.

Both contrast a Spirit-related understanding of circumcision with reliance on flesh. Philippians names worship by the Spirit of God and boasting in Christ; Romans names the heart, Spirit rather than letter, and praise from God. Their particular clauses remain distinct rather than being rewritten as one identical formula.

review_notes: All61 complete Romans1–2 original source units were read in a complete1972-token view, after all1003 original Acts units were confirmed read at07:09:16UTC. The complete433-unit Romans inventory was prepared before Romans source reading at07:10:14UTC and earns zero completion credit.

All61 actual retained target/context comparisons were read in six complete ordered views of2492,2985,2595,2479,2654 and2457 tokens (the last view covers11 rather than10 sources). No truncated body is used as reading evidence; exact repeated ranges may be reused only after complete actual reading.

Two prospective Exodus target identities were corrected after actual body comparison: the supplied edition has adultery at20:13, theft at20:14 and murder at20:15. Final target IDs use those actual units; no conventional numbering is substituted.

Habakkuk2:4 says My faithfulness while Romans1:17 says faith; Jeremiah38:33 names My laws while Romans2:15 names the work of the law. Psalms retain Greek identities105:20,95:13 and61:13. Those actual texts and distinctions remain intact.

Creator/creation knowledge comparisons preserve Wisdom13's small-blame and not-excusable clauses. Impurity comparisons distinguish divine handing-over from people handing themselves over; the female/male relation is an internal comparison rather than an added female-specific Leviticus prohibition.

The law, circumcision and judgment comparisons preserve different audiences, conditional forms and consequences. Later Romans passages and other letters are retained targets/context only: Romans3–16 source reviews and every1Corinthians source review remain pending. Next new source is Romans3:1.
The independent61-pair peer preserved Philippians3:3 worship by the Spirit of God in the2:29 rationale, distinct from Romans in Spirit. No source outcome, target or count changed.
